source.title: Let Me Grok for You: Accelerating Grokking via Embedding Transfer from a Weaker Model
source.authors: Zhiwei Xu; Zhi-Yu Ni; Yixin Wang; Wei Hu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports training and test dynamics on grokking tasks, including standard-training comparisons, but uses different models and embedding-transfer experiments rather than reproducing the original study's full method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own reported training dynamics, embedding comparisons, and initialization-sensitive feature finding. Reported hyperparameter choices are not treated as results. Claims about prior work in the related-work section are not rows.
record.test_reason: GrokTransfer is mainly a mitigation method, but the paper reports its own standard-training results on whether delay appears. Section 2.1 varies the input embedding on modular addition: one-hot and GPT embeddings grok, while binary and Fourier embeddings generalize continuously. It also reproduces delayed generalization on XOR cluster data and states that grokking persists after tuning initialization scale. These bear on V1's scope and on V3's initialization-scale account, using a different method from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' key claim is that data embedding critically determines whether generalization is delayed. Transferring an embedding from a weaker, partially generalizing model removes the delay: this is proved for XOR after one GD step and shown empirically for FNNs and Transformers on algorithmic tasks. The initialization-scale point is a secondary remark that the kernel regime may not be the sole cause.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies embedding transfer from a weaker model and compares the resulting dynamics with training from scratch; it does not reproduce the original grokking experiment as its central method.
record.method_sensitivity: Embedding type changes whether modular-addition training shows a sharp transition; embedding transfer changes target-model dynamics. Learned XOR features are initialization-sensitive. The paper also reports tuning initialization scale but gives no numerical sweep results.

fits_no_version.finding: Empirical NTK change evolves similarly across all four embeddings, although only some of them grok.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether delayed generalization occurs depends on the input embedding or representation, and kernel-change measures do not distinguish grokking from non-grokking runs.

record.problems: Empirical curves are mostly presented as figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The training-set-size delay relationship is not tested. The initialization-scale claim is stated without numerical sweep results. Some appended non-algorithmic results are figure-only and lack textual interpretation.

untested.parts: The claim that the delay grows as the training set shrinks: all modular runs use a 25% training fraction.
Gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, and progress measures. Only an empirical-NTK change is reported, and it is not a circuit measure.

Grokking on images, text or molecules under standard training (the MNIST curve is figure only). Switching the delay on or off by weight norm on non-algorithmic data. A direct test of the lazy-to-rich account.
All of it. Weight decay is only grid-searched, and there is no critical dataset size or ungrokking.
Whether different architectures or hyperparameters converge to the same algorithm.
All of it. The paper uses float32 and AdamW and mentions slingshot oscillations, but does not control for them.

missing.what: 8-layer Transformer trained from scratch on modular addition shows a generalization delay: about 10000 epochs to generalize versus about 1000 with GrokTransfer, and wall-clock time 392667 ms.
2-layer and 4-layer Transformers trained from scratch on (40,3)-parity show no delayed generalization.
Binary embedding fails to reduce the sharp phase transition on modular multiplication, though it does on addition.
Fig. 1b standard training shows a clear phase transition, but only learning rate and weight decay were tuned there, not init scale. This matters when reading R18.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is primarily a mitigation method, so most comparator rows (R11–R14, R16) are its own method and are unlinked. The V6 challenge was removed because the initialization sensitivity is a symmetry choice among equivalent features in a capacity-limited model. The R18 evidence is selection-based; a researcher should check the grid range (0.1–1.5) and note that the selection criterion favours fast generalization.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not sweep training-set size to test whether smaller sets require more optimization.
It does not track a generalizing circuit forming gradually, memorizing components being removed, or continuous circuit-level progress anticipating a jump.
It reports a delayed-generalization XOR setting and an MNIST experiment, but does not establish a general initialization-scale or weight-norm switch, or test the lazy-to-rich account.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is tested.
The paper does not test whether low-norm bias selects an efficient circuit, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
The reported feature-variation finding is limited to the three-neuron XOR weak model; the paper does not compare identifiable algorithms across a broad range of architectures and hyperparameters.
The paper does not test whether grokking disappears when adaptive-optimizer instabilities or softmax floating-point limits are controlled.

rows.subject: three-layer FNN, width=512
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular addition using Fourier embeddings
rows.value: The text says generalization progresses continuously and the model can simultaneously achieve memorization and perfect generalization; numerical accuracy values are figure only.
rows.note: This condition is explicitly described as having no sharp delayed transition.
rows.check: Memorization and generalization happen together, so there is no delay; this is absent, not reversed. The Fourier embedding builds the task solution into the input, which explains the result.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network, hidden width 2048
rows.operation_detail: Standard training on XOR cluster data
rows.value: Overfitting is achieved by the fifth epoch and generalization begins around the 80-th epoch.
rows.note: This is a delayed-generalization result on synthetic XOR cluster data, not an algorithmic-table task.
rows.check: XOR cluster data is synthetic and parity-like, not images, text or molecules, so the link to V3 is borderline. It reproduces the Xu et al. 2024 setting with full-batch GD and weight decay 0.1. Initialization scale was not varied.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, final paragraph; Figure 4(a); Appendix A.3.2.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network, hidden width 3
rows.operation_detail: Train the small XOR weak model
rows.value: Test accuracy around 75%; a phase transition near the 100th epoch is observed.
rows.note: The paper attributes the accuracy ceiling to the model's three-neuron capacity.
rows.check: This is GrokTransfer's three-neuron weak model, whose accuracy is capped at 75% by capacity (Lemma 3.1). The cap reflects expressivity, not a weaker grokking effect. It is a component of the method, not an independent test.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network, hidden width 3
rows.operation_detail: Inspect learned first-layer feature directions across initializations
rows.value: The specific features learned are sensitive to initialization; empirically, the model learns three among the four feature directions when test accuracy is around 75%.
rows.note: This is evidence of initialization-dependent feature selection in this weak model, not a broad comparison of complete algorithms.
rows.check: The paper says the learned features are always three of the four symmetric XOR directions. Only which three varies with initialization, which is the same solution up to symmetry, not a different algorithm. The model is also capacity-limited. This cannot show the algorithm differing across runs, so the challenges label is unwarranted.

rows.subject: FNN on modular addition
rows.operation_detail: Tune initialization scale as part of hyperparameter selection
rows.value: The authors state that grokking persists even after carefully tuning the initialization scale.
rows.note: No numerical results for an initialization-scale sweep are supplied in the text.
rows.check: Grid-searched initialization scale (0.1–1.5) does not remove grokking for one-hot or GPT embeddings; the selected one-hot configuration uses init 0.2. This is a statement from hyperparameter selection (fastest to 90% validation accuracy), with no sweep curves. For V3's switch-off-by-init-scale part the effect is absent, not observed.
